name: Tramadol
monitoring: Pain scores, respiratory rate, sedation level, seizure risk
patient_counselling: Dual mechanism: weak mu-opioid + SNRI. Seizure risk at high doses. Avoid alcohol.
mechanism_of_action: Weak mu-opioid receptor agonist + inhibits norepinephrine and serotonin reuptake, providing dual analgesic mechanism.
warnings: Risk of respiratory depression in CYP2D6 poor metabolizers
overdose: Symptoms: seizures, serotonin syndrome, respiratory depression, agitated delirium. Management: naloxone (may require higher doses), benzodiazepines for seizures.
pharmacokinetics: Oral bioavailability: 68%. t1/2: 6h (tramadol), 7h (O-desmethyl metabolite). CYP2D6 → active metabolite (M1). Renal excretion.
clinical_pearls: 50x less potent than morphine
CYP2D6 ultrarapid metabolizers: higher risk of toxicity
Combined with acetaminophen in Ultracet

name: Milnacipran

dosage.adult: Start 12.5mg PO daily, titrate to 25mg BID over 1 week

monitoring: BP, pain scores, mood, heart rate
patient_counselling: Take with food. Do not stop abruptly. Monitor BP.
mechanism_of_action: SNRI with greater affinity for norepinephrine than serotonin reuptake inhibition. NE:5-HT ratio approximately 3:1.
overdose: Symptoms: serotonin syndrome, tachycardia, hypertension. Management: supportive care, cyproheptadine.
pharmacokinetics: Oral bioavailability: 85%. t1/2: 8h. Minimal hepatic metabolism. Renal excretion (50-60%).
clinical_pearls: NE-predominant SNRI — better for pain than depression
Only FDA-approved for fibromyalgia (not depression in US)
Less sexual dysfunction than SSRIs

name: Capsaicin topical

dosage.adult: 0.025-0.075% cream: apply TID-QID. 8% patch: single application by healthcare provider

monitoring: Pain scores, skin integrity, local reactions
patient_counselling: Initial burning is expected and decreases with continued use. Wash hands thoroughly after application.
mechanism_of_action: Depletes substance P from sensory neurons via TRPV1 receptor activation, reducing pain signaling. Initial activation followed by desensitization.
overdose: Symptoms: severe local burning. Management: wash with soap and olive oil (not water initially).
pharmacokinetics: Topical absorption minimal. Local action primarily. High-dose patch (8%) provides 3 months pain relief.
clinical_pearls: Qutenza 8% patch applied in clinic for PHN — single application provides 3 months relief
Initial worsening expected — counsel patients
Mechanism: defunctionalizes nociceptors by depleting substance P
Also used for diabetic peripheral neuropathy of feet

name: Lidocaine patch
contraindications: Broken or irritated skin at application site

dosage.adult: 1-3 patches applied to intact skin for 12h on/12h off (max 3 patches/12h period)

monitoring: Pain scores, skin integrity, plasma lidocaine levels if multiple patches
patient_counselling: Apply to intact skin only. Remove before MRI. Can cut patches if needed.
mechanism_of_action: Blocks voltage-gated sodium channels in peripheral sensory neurons, preventing nerve impulse generation and propagation.
warnings: Plasma levels increase with more patches
overdose: Symptoms: CNS excitation then depression, cardiovascular collapse (rare with topical). Management: airway management, benzodiazepines.
pharmacokinetics: Systemic absorption minimal (<5% of dose). Peak plasma: 13h. Duration: up to 12h after removal.
clinical_pearls: Apply to area of maximum pain
Up to 3 patches can be worn simultaneously
Can cut patches to fit smaller areas
No systemic toxicity at recommended dose

name: Diclofenac topical

dosage.adult: Apply 4g to affected joint QID (max 32g/day for knee)

patient_counselling: Apply to clean, dry skin. Do not use with occlusive dressings. Avoid eyes and mucous membranes.
mechanism_of_action: Topical NSAID — inhibits COX-2 locally, reducing prostaglandin-mediated inflammation at application site.
warnings: Systemic absorption possible with large areas
overdose: Symptoms: local irritation. Management: wash area with water.
pharmacokinetics: Systemic absorption <6%. Local tissue concentrations higher than plasma. Minimal systemic effects.
clinical_pearls: Pennsaid: diclofenac in DMSO solution for deeper penetration
Less GI toxicity than oral NSAIDs
Good alternative for patients who cannot tolerate oral NSAIDs
Solaraze 3%: for actinic keratosis (sun-damaged skin)

name: Phenylbutazone

dosage.adult: 100mg TID with food, reduce to lowest effective dose

monitoring: CBC weekly for first month, LFTs, renal function, fluid balance
patient_counselling: Take with food. Report sore throat, fever, bruising immediately (blood dyscrasia signs).
mechanism_of_action: Non-selective COX inhibitor with potent anti-inflammatory and uricosuric effects.
overdose: Symptoms: nausea, vomiting, GI bleeding, CNS depression. Management: supportive care.
pharmacokinetics: Oral bioavailability: high. t1/2: 12h (but active metabolites 3 days). Protein binding: 98%. Hepatic metabolism.
black_box_warnings: Risk of serious GI adverse events
clinical_pearls: Rarely used in humans due to toxicity profile
Still used in veterinary medicine (horses)
Uricosuric effect — useful in gout
Monitor CBC closely in first month

name: Nabumetone

dosage.adult: 1000mg PO daily, may increase to 2000mg/day in divided doses

patient_counselling: Take with food. Prodrug — converted to active metabolite in GI wall.
mechanism_of_action: Non-selective COX inhibitor prodrug. Converted to 6-MNA (active metabolite) in GI wall and liver.
overdose: Symptoms: GI upset. Management: supportive care.
pharmacokinetics: Oral bioavailability: 35% (as active metabolite). t1/2: 22h (active metabolite). Hepatic metabolism.
clinical_pearls: Prodrug — less direct GI irritation
Once or twice daily dosing
Lower GI toxicity than most NSAIDs
Good choice for patients with GI sensitivity to other NSAIDs

name: Fenoprofen
patient_counselling: Take with food or milk. Report decreased urine output.
mechanism_of_action: Non-selective COX-1/COX-2 inhibitor reducing prostaglandin synthesis.
overdose: Symptoms: nausea, vomiting, headache. Management: supportive care.
pharmacokinetics: Oral bioavailability: 85%. t1/2: 3h. Hepatic metabolism. Protein binding: 99%.
clinical_pearls: Higher protein binding than other propionic acid NSAIDs
Interstitial nephritis reported more with fenoprofen
Good analgesic for mild-moderate pain

name: Ketoprofen
patient_counselling: Take with food. Available as ER formulation for once-daily dosing.
mechanism_of_action: Non-selective COX-1/COX-2 inhibitor with potent analgesic and anti-inflammatory properties.
overdose: Symptoms: GI upset, drowsiness. Management: supportive care.
pharmacokinetics: Oral bioavailability: 90%. t1/2: 3-5h. Hepatic metabolism. Protein binding: 99%.
clinical_pearls: Good for dysmenorrhea
Available as topical gel (Solaraze-like formulations in some countries)
ER formulation allows once-daily dosing

name: Oxaprozin
patient_counselling: Take with food. Once-daily dosing.
mechanism_of_action: Non-selective COX-1/COX-2 inhibitor with long half-life allowing once-daily dosing.
overdose: Symptoms: GI upset. Management: supportive care.
pharmacokinetics: Oral bioavailability: 95%. t1/2: 40-60h. Hepatic metabolism (CYP2C9). Protein binding: 99%.
clinical_pearls: Long half-life — once-daily dosing
Similar efficacy to naproxen
Good for compliance with chronic conditions

name: Flurbiprofen
patient_counselling: Take with food. Available as ophthalmic solution for intraoperative miosis prevention.
mechanism_of_action: Non-selective COX-1/COX-2 inhibitor reducing prostaglandin synthesis.
overdose: Symptoms: GI upset. Management: supportive care.
pharmacokinetics: Oral bioavailability: 96%. t1/2: 5-6h. Hepatic metabolism. Protein binding: 99%.
clinical_pearls: Ophthalmic solution (Ocufen) used intraoperatively to prevent miosis
Good analgesic with moderate half-life
Propionic acid derivative — similar class to ibuprofen and naproxen

name: Sulindac
patient_counselling: Take with food. Prodrug — requires hepatic activation. Report jaundice or dark urine.
mechanism_of_action: Prodrug converted to active sulfide metabolite, which inhibits COX. Also has COX-independent anti-tumor effects.
overdose: Symptoms: GI upset, drowsiness. Management: supportive care.
pharmacokinetics: Oral bioavailability: 50% (as active metabolite). t1/2: 7-8h (active metabolite 16h). Hepatic metabolism.
clinical_pearls: Prodrug — active metabolite has longer half-life
Chemopreventive properties for colorectal cancer/polyps
May reduce GI toxicity compared to non-prodrug NSAIDs
Hepatotoxicity — monitor LFTs

name: Tolmetin
patient_counselling: Take with food or milk.
mechanism_of_action: Non-selective COX-1/COX-2 inhibitor.
overdose: Symptoms: GI upset. Management: supportive care.
pharmacokinetics: Oral bioavailability: high. t1/2: 1-2h. Hepatic metabolism. Protein binding: 99%.
clinical_pearls: Short half-life requiring TID dosing
Used in JIA
Acetic acid derivative — similar to indomethacin and diclofenac

name: Etodolac
patient_counselling: Take with food. Short-term use preferred.
mechanism_of_action: Preferential COX-2 inhibitor with less COX-1 inhibition, potentially lower GI toxicity.
overdose: Symptoms: GI upset. Management: supportive care.
pharmacokinetics: Oral bioavailability: high. t1/2: 6-7h. Hepatic metabolism. Protein binding: 99%.
clinical_pearls: COX-2 preferential — less GI toxicity than non-selective NSAIDs
Short-term analgesic use preferred
Good option for acute pain

name: Nefopam
patient_counselling: Non-narcotic analgesic. May cause drowsiness. Avoid MAOIs.
mechanism_of_action: Inhibits reuptake of serotonin, norepinephrine, and dopamine in CNS. Also has NMDA receptor antagonist properties.
overdose: Symptoms: seizures, serotonin syndrome, tachycardia. Management: supportive care.
pharmacokinetics: Oral bioavailability: 36%. t1/2: 4-5h. Hepatic metabolism. Protein binding: 71%.
clinical_pearls: Non-opioid, non-NSAID analgesic
Commonly used in Europe and Asia, not available in US
Good opioid-sparing agent
Intranasal formulation available

name: Paracetamol IV
monitoring: LFTs, hepatic function, temperature, pain scores
patient_counselling: IV formulation provides rapid onset. Monitor for signs of liver injury.
mechanism_of_action: Inhibits COX-2 centrally and in spinal cord. Also activates descending serotonergic pathways. Exact mechanism not fully understood.
warnings: Hepatotoxicity risk especially with alcohol use or malnutrition
Rapid IV infusion may cause hypotension
overdose: Symptoms: nausea, vomiting, right upper quadrant pain, hepatic failure. Management: N-acetylcysteine (NAC) within 8 hours.
pharmacokinetics: IV bioavailability: 100%. Onset: 5-10 min. t1/2: 2-3h. Hepatic metabolism (CYP2E1). Renal excretion.
black_box_warnings: Risk of severe hepatotoxicity in overdose
clinical_pearls: IV formulation: 1g over 15 min
Faster onset than oral for acute pain
Max 4g/day in healthy adults, 2g/day in liver disease or alcohol use
NAC is the antidote — most effective within 8 hours of overdose

name: Aspirin (low-dose)
monitoring: Signs of bleeding, GI symptoms, tinnitus
patient_counselling: Take with food. Do not take ibuprofen at same time (blocks cardioprotective effect).
mechanism_of_action: Irreversibly acetylates COX-1 in platelets, blocking thromboxane A2 synthesis and platelet aggregation for platelet lifetime (~10 days).
overdose: Symptoms: tinnitus, hearing loss, metabolic acidosis, hyperventilation, CNS depression. Management: sodium bicarbonate, activated charcoal.
pharmacokinetics: Oral bioavailability: 68%. t1/2: 15-20 min (aspirin), 2-3h (salicylate). Irreversible platelet inhibition.
black_box_warnings: Risk of hemorrhagic stroke (with high doses)
clinical_pearls: 75-100mg is optimal antiplatelet dose
Higher doses needed for anti-inflammatory effect
Do NOT give to children <16 with viral illness (Reye syndrome)
Ibuprofen taken before aspirin blocks cardioprotective effect

name: Celecoxib/Acetaminophen
patient_counselling: Take with food. Do not exceed 4g acetaminophen/day from all sources.
mechanism_of_action: Dual COX-2 inhibition (peripheral inflammation) + central analgesic (acetaminophen) providing additive pain relief.
overdose: Symptoms: GI upset, hepatotoxicity. Management: NAC for acetaminophen component.
pharmacokinetics: Combination product — individual pharmacokinetics apply.
clinical_pearls: Combination provides additive analgesia
Lower NSAID dose needed when combined with acetaminophen
Good for patients who need multi-modal pain management

name: Tramadol/Acetaminophen

dosage.adult: Tramadol 37.5mg + Acetaminophen 325mg, 1-2 tabs PO q4-6h PRN (max 8 tabs/day)

monitoring: Pain scores, respiratory rate, sedation, liver function
patient_counselling: Do not exceed 3g acetaminophen/day from all sources. Avoid alcohol.
mechanism_of_action: Dual mechanism: weak mu-opioid agonist + SNRI (tramadol) combined with central COX inhibition (acetaminophen).
overdose: Symptoms: seizures, serotonin syndrome, hepatotoxicity. Management: naloxone, NAC.
pharmacokinetics: Tramadol: t1/2 6h. Acetaminophen: t1/2 2-3h. Both hepatically metabolized.
clinical_pearls: Reduces tramadol dose needed — less seizure risk
Common post-surgical combination
Max 8 tablets/day to limit acetaminophen intake

name: Hydrocodone/Acetaminophen
contraindications: Acute or severe GI paralytic ileus

dosage.adult: Hydrocodone 2.5-10mg + Acetaminophen 300-325mg PO q4-6h PRN (max 6 tabs/day)

monitoring: Pain scores, respiratory rate, sedation, bowel function
patient_counselling: Take as directed. Do not exceed 4g acetaminophen/day from all sources. Avoid alcohol.
mechanism_of_action: Mu-opioid receptor agonist (hydrocodone) + central COX inhibition (acetaminophen).
overdose: Symptoms: respiratory depression, CNS depression, hepatotoxicity. Management: naloxone, NAC.
pharmacokinetics: Hydrocodone: t1/2 4h. Acetaminophen: t1/2 2-3h. Hepatic metabolism.
black_box_warnings: Risk of addiction, abuse, and misuse
clinical_pearls: Schedule II opioid (reclassified from III in 2014)
Most prescribed opioid in US historically
Norco preferred over Vicodin (lower acetaminophen content)

name: Oxycodone/Acetaminophen
contraindications: Acute or severe GI paralytic ileus

dosage.adult: Oxycodone 2.5-10mg + Acetaminophen 325mg PO q4-6h PRN (max 6 tabs/day)

monitoring: Pain scores, respiratory rate, sedation, bowel function
patient_counselling: Take as directed. Do not exceed 4g acetaminophen/day. Avoid alcohol.
mechanism_of_action: Mu-opioid receptor agonist (oxycodone) + central COX inhibition (acetaminophen).
overdose: Symptoms: respiratory depression, hepatotoxicity. Management: naloxone, NAC.
pharmacokinetics: Oxycodone: t1/2 3-4.5h. Acetaminophen: t1/2 2-3h. Hepatic metabolism.
black_box_warnings: Risk of addiction, abuse, and misuse
clinical_pearls: More potent per mg than hydrocodone
Available in generic, reducing cost
Percocet reformulated to limit tablet abuse

name: Codeine/Acetaminophen
patient_counselling: Prodrug — effectiveness depends on CYP2D6 metabolism. Some patients cannot convert to active morphine.
mechanism_of_action: Codeine (prodrug) → CYP2D6 → morphine (active) for mu-opioid agonism. Acetaminophen provides central analgesia.
warnings: Respiratory depression in CYP2D6 ultrarapid metabolizers
overdose: Symptoms: respiratory depression, hepatotoxicity. Management: naloxone, NAC.
pharmacokinetics: Codeine: t1/2 3h. Prodrug → morphine via CYP2D6. Acetaminophen: t1/2 2-3h.
clinical_pearls: CYP2D6 polymorphism makes response unpredictable
FDA black box: not recommended in children <12 for pain
30% of population are CYP2D6 poor metabolizers — codeine ineffective
6-7% are ultrarapid metabolizers — risk of toxicity

name: Tramadol/Sumatriptan

dosage.adult: As formulated in clinical trials (investigational combination)

monitoring: BP, neurological status, serotonin syndrome signs
patient_counselling: Avoid alcohol. Report chest pain, shortness of breath.
mechanism_of_action: Dual 5-HT agonism (sumatriptan) + opioid agonism/SNRI (tramadol) targeting multiple migraine pathways.
overdose: Symptoms: serotonin syndrome, respiratory depression. Management: supportive care.
pharmacokinetics: Both hepatically metabolized.
clinical_pearls: Combination targets both vascular and central migraine mechanisms
Investigational combination
Similar concept to Cafergot (ergotamine/caffeine)

name: Butorphanol

dosage.adult: IM/IV: 1-4mg q3-4h PRN. Nasal: 1mg q3-4h (max 4 doses/day)

patient_counselling: Nasal spray: blow nose first, insert tip, inhale. May cause bitter taste.
mechanism_of_action: Kappa agonist / partial mu agonist / weak mu antagonist. Provides analgesia with less respiratory depression than full agonists.
overdose: Symptoms: respiratory depression, CNS depression. Management: naloxone.
pharmacokinetics: IM onset: 10min. IV onset: minutes. t1/2: 4-5h. Nasal bioavailability: 60-70%. Hepatic metabolism.
clinical_pearls: Kappa agonism provides analgesia without full mu effects
Nasal formulation useful when IV access unavailable
Less euphoria than full agonists — less abuse potential
Mixed agonist-antagonist — caution in opioid-tolerant patients

name: Pentazocine
monitoring: Pain scores, respiratory rate, sedation, psychological effects
patient_counselling: May cause hallucinations or dysphoria. Avoid driving.
mechanism_of_action: Kappa agonist / partial mu agonist. Produces analgesia with ceiling effect for respiratory depression.
overdose: Symptoms: CNS depression, respiratory depression, psychotomimetic effects. Management: naloxone.
pharmacokinetics: Oral bioavailability: 50-60%. t1/2: 2-3h. Hepatic metabolism.
clinical_pearls: Ceiling effect for respiratory depression
Kappa agonism — dysphoric and hallucinogenic effects
Less commonly used due to psychotomimetic effects
Schedule IV controlled substance

name: Meperidine
monitoring: Pain scores, respiratory rate, seizure activity, mental status
patient_counselling: Short-term use only. Do not use with MAOIs. Report tremors or seizures.
mechanism_of_action: Mu-opioid receptor agonist with local anesthetic properties. Active metabolite (normeperidine) is neurotoxic.
overdose: Symptoms: seizures, respiratory depression, serotonin syndrome (if with serotonergic drugs). Management: naloxone, benzodiazepines for seizures.
pharmacokinetics: Oral bioavailability: 50%. t1/2: 3h (meperidine), 15-30h (normeperidine). Hepatic metabolism.
clinical_pearls: AVOID in chronic pain — normeperidine causes seizures
Use limited to acute setting (e.g., post-surgical shivering)
Active metabolite normeperidine accumulates with renal impairment
Not equivalent to morphine — 10mg meperidine ≈ 1.5mg morphine

name: Fentanyl sublingual
contraindications: Acute or severe GI paralytic ileus

dosage.adult: 200mcg SL, titrate in 200mcg increments to effective dose. Max 4 doses per breakthrough episode.

patient_counselling: Place tablet under tongue until dissolved. Do not chew or swallow. Avoid eating/drinking for 10 min.
mechanism_of_action: Synthetic mu-opioid receptor agonist, 50-100x more potent than morphine. Rapid onset via sublingual absorption.
overdose: Symptoms: respiratory depression, CNS depression, miosis. Management: naloxone.
pharmacokinetics: SL bioavailability: 51%. Onset: 5-15 min. Duration: 1-2h. Hepatic metabolism (CYP3A4).
black_box_warnings: Risk of addiction, abuse, and misuse
Risk of fatal overdose from accidental ingestion
clinical_pearls: 50-100x more potent than morphine
Only for breakthrough cancer pain in opioid-tolerant patients
Available as sublingual tablet (Abstral) and oral film (Onsolis)
Must be opioid-tolerant (on ≥60mg morphine equivalent daily)

name: Hydromorphone
contraindications: Acute or severe GI paralytic ileus

dosage.adult: Oral: 2-4mg q4-6h PRN. IV: 0.2-1mg q2-3h PRN. ER: 8mg q12h, titrate.

monitoring: Pain scores, respiratory rate, sedation, bowel function
patient_counselling: More potent than morphine (4x). Do not crush ER formulation.
mechanism_of_action: Pure mu-opioid receptor agonist. 4-8x more potent than morphine.
overdose: Symptoms: respiratory depression, CNS depression. Management: naloxone.
pharmacokinetics: Oral bioavailability: 30-40%. t1/2: 2-3h. Hepatic metabolism (glucuronidation).
black_box_warnings: Risk of addiction, abuse, and misuse
clinical_pearls: 4x more potent than morphine (oral equivalency: 1.5mg HM ≈ morphine 6mg)
Dilaudid (IV) is commonly requested by drug-seeking patients — 'Dilaudid' is a red flag term
ER formulation: Exalgo (once-daily dosing)
No active metabolites — safe in renal impairment (preferred over morphine)

name: Oxymorphone
contraindications: Acute or severe GI paralytic ileus

dosage.adult: IR: 5-10mg PO q4-6h. ER: 5-10mg q12h. Rectal: 5mg PR q6h.

patient_counselling: Available as oral and rectal formulations. Do not crush ER.
mechanism_of_action: Pure mu-opioid receptor agonist. 3-7x more potent than morphine.
overdose: Symptoms: respiratory depression, CNS depression. Management: naloxone.
pharmacokinetics: Oral bioavailability: 10% (high first-pass). t1/2: 7-9h. Hepatic metabolism (glucuronidation).
black_box_warnings: Risk of addiction, abuse, and misuse
clinical_pearls: Very high first-pass metabolism — oral bioavailability only 10%
Opana ER withdrawn from US market (2017) due to abuse via injection
Rectal formulation bypasses first-pass metabolism
Active metabolites in renal impairment — use with caution

name: Levorphanol
patient_counselling: Available in limited supply. Long-acting analgesic.
mechanism_of_action: Mu-opioid agonist + NMDA receptor antagonist + SNRI — triple mechanism analgesic.
overdose: Symptoms: respiratory depression. Management: naloxone.
pharmacokinetics: Oral bioavailability: variable. t1/2: 12-16h. Hepatic metabolism.
clinical_pearls: NMDA antagonist properties — good for neuropathic pain
Long half-life — less frequent dosing
Racemic mixture — levorphanol is the active enantiomer of racemorphan
Triple mechanism: opioid + NMDA antagonist + SNRI
